question.text: Scenario: Vikram (age 32) is a software engineer earning Rs. 18,00,000 per annum. His wife Priya (age 30) also works and earns Rs. 8,00,000 per annum. They have one child aged 2 years, who is their only dependent. They own a house valued at Rs. 40,00,000 with an outstanding home loan of Rs. 15,00,000. Their current investments include: Rs. 5,00,000 in bank fixed deposits, Rs. 3,00,000 in equity mutual funds, Rs. 2,00,000 in PPF, and an emergency fund of Rs. 1,50,000. Vikram has roughly 10 years of active investing experience and currently holds investments across equity, debt, gold (sovereign gold bonds) and international funds; he reports being comfortable holding investments through a 30%+ market drawdown. Their financial goals are: child's higher education (16 years away), retirement (28 years away), and a car upgrade (2 years away). Vikram's investment adviser Suresh administers the firm's risk profiling questionnaire. Question 1 of 5: Based on Vikram's overall profile — long investment experience, holdings across a wide range of products, dual income, young age, low dependents, long time horizons, and demonstrated tolerance for sizeable drawdowns — which risk profile category under the 3-grade classification (Conservative / Moderate / Aggressive) does the NISM Series X-B workbook (pp. 411-414) BEST support for Vikram?

answer.text: Conservative — since he has a home loan liability of Rs. 15,00,000
Moderate — since he has a young child to support
Aggressive — given long investment experience, range of products held, dual income, young age, low dependents, long time horizons, and tolerance for sizeable drawdowns
Conservative-Moderate — since his emergency fund is only Rs. 1,50,000

explanation.text: The Logic: NISM Series X-B workbook pp. 411-414 list the source-backed factors that increase risk appetite: long investment experience, holdings across a range of products, dual/strong income, young age, few dependents, long time horizons, and demonstrated tolerance for market drawdowns. Vikram exhibits all of these, which is exactly the workbook's profile of an aggressive investor. The Trap: Options A and D pick on isolated negatives (home loan; modest emergency fund) but the workbook treats risk appetite as a holistic assessment across all factors, not a deduction for a single weakness. Option B treats one dependent in a dual-income household as risk-reducing — not significant enough to push him out of aggressive. The audit flagged the original because it keyed Aggressive on a 72/100 score threshold that does not appear in the workbook. Note: The original stem keyed Aggressive on an unsupported 72/100 score threshold. The scenario now adds workbook-backed evidence (long investment experience, a wide range of products held, and tolerance for drawdowns) that the workbook explicitly associates with aggressive investors, removing reliance on the unsupported numeric cutoff. Option C is uniquely supported.
